newsitem.title: USA: Northeast sees no reason to shut Millstone.
newsitem.headline: Northeast sees no reason to shut Millstone.

text.p: Northeast Utilities officials said Monday it would not make economic sense to permanently shut down the company's troubled Millstone 1 and 2 nuclear power plants.

Northeast Nuclear President and Chief Executive Officer Bruce Kenyon told a news conference that Millstone units 1 and 2 have a combined net present value to customers of $570 million that would be lost if the plants were decommissioned.

Kenyon said the Berlin, Conn.-based utility will file an economic analysis with state regulators Tuesday saying that Millstone 2 has a net present value of $500 million and $70 million for the adjacent unit, Millstone 1.
A third unit at the Millstone site, the 1,150 megawatt (MW) Millstone 3, was not studied because its economic viability was not questioned by the company.
All three units have been idled since March, 1996, amid safety concerns raised by the federal Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC).

"There has been a lot of speculation on units 1 and 2 that they are never coming back on line. So the news is that based on a reasonable set of assumptions, we believe they both have economic value," Jeff Kotkin, director of investor relations for Northeast Utilities, told Reuters after the news conference.
Kotkins said the 660 MW Millstone 1 is licensed for another 13 years and Millstone 2, rated at 870 MW, has another 18 years before its current operating license expires.
Kenyon said he did not expect any change in the recovery schedule for the three Millstone plants, which are slated to come back on line by early 1998, pending NRC approval.

He said the Conn. Department of Public Utility Control's decision last week rejecting Northeast's request to recover up to $340 million of the cost of the Millstone outages by raising electricity rates was not a financial setback for Northeast's nuclear division.
Northeast's latest estimates put the cost of the outages, including buying replacement power from other producers, at about $990 million.
"The funding of the recovery for the Millstone units did not depend on a successful outcome of this (DPUC) case," Kenyon said.
"As the CEO of Northeast Nuclear, I feel I have the funds to restart these units properly," he added.
